passage:
Week one, Monday: The science fair topics went up. Anand chose water filters and told Disha it would be easy. "I'll start this weekend." He didn't. Every time he opened the notebook he pictured the judges frowning, and Disha's model from last year, and closed it again. "I work better at the end anyway," he said.
Week three, Wednesday: Four days left. Disha asked to see his plan. "Still thinking," he said, and switched the talk to cricket.
Fair day, Saturday: Anand's filter leaked on the table. The poster had spelling mistakes he would have caught with a spare hour. A judge was kind: the idea was good, the testing was thin. Walking home he told Disha, quietly, "If I'd started early and it was bad, that would really be me. This way it's just the rushing."

qa.q: What did the judge say about Anand's project?
qa.a: That the idea was good and the testing was thin.

qa.q: Why did Anand keep closing the notebook?
qa.a: Opening it made him picture frowning judges and Disha's strong model; not starting kept him from finding out he might not be good enough, which felt safer.

qa.q: What was the turning point Anand missed, and what could he try next time?
qa.a: Week one, when the dread first showed; building a rough first filter early and showing it to one person would bring feedback while there was still time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Disha see Anand's "Still thinking" in week three?
qa.a: Disha may sense he is stuck and uneasy and feel unsure whether to push or leave him be; only his confession on the way home explains what Disha couldn't see.

grounding: A teenager delays a science project to avoid being judged, which protects his self-image but leaves the project rushed.

passage: Nikita, beta, come sit. You say you'll do the history project later? Let me tell you about your Dadu at fifteen. Our headmaster announced an essay competition, and my teacher said, "Gautam, you write well, you must enter." I was so proud, and so scared. What if I wrote it and it was ordinary? Then everyone would know I wasn't special. So I didn't write. I told myself I was collecting ideas. I played carrom, I cleaned my bicycle twice. The night before, I wrote it by lantern in two hours. It won nothing. And the worst part, Nikita, was that I never learned whether I was any good, because what I handed in wasn't me really trying. So start yours ugly, today. Ugly can be fixed.

qa.q: What did Gautam's teacher say about the essay competition?
qa.a: "Gautam, you write well, you must enter."

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel both proud and scared?
qa.a: The praise made him proud but raised the stakes: an ordinary essay would prove he wasn't special, so not writing felt like protecting the teacher's good opinion.

qa.q: What choice does Dadu urge Nikita to make?
qa.a: To start the history project today, even roughly, since an ugly first draft can be fixed while a last-night rush leaves no room to improve.

qa.q: What might Nikita take from hearing Dadu admit this?
qa.a: Nikita may feel less alone with the fear of being judged, and a grandfather owning up to his own mistake makes the advice feel like help rather than a scolding.

grounding: A grandfather recalls delaying an essay at fifteen to avoid a verdict on his ability, which made the final essay worse.

passage: Sarika had three weeks to send four drawings for the district art scholarship. Her older cousin had won it once, and everyone at home said, "Your turn now." Sarika kept her sketchbook shut. "The light's bad in the evenings," she told Irawati, which was true: the power in their lane went off most nights. But she didn't draw on bright Sunday afternoons either. She sorted her pencils, watched videos of other artists and said she was waiting to feel inspired. With four days left, the power cuts got worse, and she drew by the torch on Irawati's phone, hurrying, smudging the charcoal. She sent the drawings at midnight. "At least if they reject it," she said, "it's because I rushed, not because I can't draw." Irawati didn't answer.

qa.q: How did Sarika light her drawings in the last four days?
qa.a: She drew by the torch on Irawati's phone.

qa.q: What does Sarika's final remark reveal about why she waited?
qa.a: She was afraid her best effort might not be good enough; rushing gave her something else to blame, which felt safer than risking a real verdict on her skill.

qa.q: How could Sarika have handled the power cuts and the fear?
qa.a: Using the bright Sunday afternoons for rough sketches, even imperfect ones, so the scary first step happened early and the power cuts mattered less.

qa.q: Why might Irawati stay silent after Sarika's remark?
qa.a: Irawati may see that the excuse hides fear and not know how to say so kindly at midnight, or may simply be worn out after lending the phone torch for days.

grounding: A teenager avoids starting a scholarship portfolio so that a poor result can be blamed on rushing, and the work suffers.

passage: The Class 10 science project was due in three weeks, and Kunal hadn't opened the kit. Every evening in their Bhopal flat he tidied his desk, sharpened pencils and watched videos of other students' models, each one better than anything he could picture making. His friend Samir had already built a solar oven. "You topped the mock," Samir said on the school bus. "Yours will be amazing." Kunal felt his throat tighten. If it wasn't amazing, everyone would know the topper was a fake. So he waited. Two nights before the deadline he finally started, with glue that wouldn't set and the stationery shop already closed. The model leaned sideways. "I didn't have time," he told the teacher, which was almost true.

qa.q: What had Samir already built?
qa.a: Samir had already built a solar oven.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's throat tighten when Samir said his model would be amazing?
qa.a: He feared an ordinary model would expose him as a 'fake' topper 😰, so not starting felt safer than finding out.

qa.q: What small step could Kunal have taken in the first week?
qa.a: Build one rough piece, like the base, with nobody watching and permission to be imperfect; starting early would have left time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Samir's praise look different if Samir knew what Kunal was feeling?
qa.a: Samir meant it kindly but might see it added pressure, and could offer to build side by side instead of predicting something amazing.

grounding: A teenager puts off a science project because a weak result would threaten his image as a topper, and the late work turns out worse.

passage:
"Simran, the debate video is due Monday. Have you recorded anything?"
"Not yet, Rekha Didi. I'm still researching."
"You've been researching for two weeks."
"It has to be good. Mrs Thomas said I have the best voice in class."
"So record a practice one. Just for me."
"No!" Simran pulled her knees up on the bed. "If it comes out bad, then she was wrong about me."
Rekha sat down beside her. "And if you record it Sunday night at eleven, what then?"
"Then it's bad because I rushed. That's different."
"Is it? Either way it's rushed, and you lose sleep too."
Simran picked at the bedsheet. "It's easier to blame the clock."
"I know. Record one line now. Just one. I'll make chai."

qa.q: Who said Simran has the best voice in class?
qa.a: Mrs Thomas said she has the best voice in class.

qa.q: What does 'It's easier to blame the clock' reveal about Simran's thinking?
qa.a: Simran is afraid of being judged: if the video is rushed, a poor result can be blamed on time rather than on her, so waiting protects her belief that she has the best voice.

qa.q: What choice does Rekha offer, and why might it work?
qa.a: Recording just one line right now, with chai; it is small enough to feel safe and breaks the wait before Sunday night makes the work worse.

qa.q: How does Rekha seem to see Simran's 'researching'?
qa.a: Rekha sees the fear under it and, rather than scolding, points out that rushing still gives a poor result, only with less sleep.

grounding: A teenager delays recording a debate video because a weak result would disprove her teacher's praise, and her sister points out the cost.
